tip: A method for squeezing video or sound into a small file, and unpacking it again.
meaning: Raw video is huge. A codec (coder-decoder) packs it into something much smaller and a player unpacks it to show. Different codecs squeeze in different ways.
example: H.264 is a codec. Your phone uses it to save videos that would otherwise fill the memory in minutes.

tip: The file "box" that holds the video, the sound and the information together.
meaning: A container (like MP4 or MKV) keeps the picture, the sound and the captions together in one file. The codecs say how each is squeezed; the container says how they are packed together.
example: A lunchbox holds a sandwich and fruit: the lunchbox is the container, the sandwich the video.

tip: An encoder makes the compressed file; a decoder opens it to play.
meaning: The encoder compresses video when you export. The decoder expands it again when you watch. Both need to speak the same codec.
example: Your computer decodes the video in real time when you press play.
vukem: An H.264 export needs an H.264 encoder. See [Encoders and presets](/docs/guide/encoders-and-presets).

tip: The kind of file, usually shown by the ending of its name, like .mp4.
meaning: The format says how the data in the file is organised. The ending of the name (the extension) is a clue, but what counts is what is inside.
example: A file named video.mp4 is in the MP4 format.

tip: The most common video file, played almost everywhere.
meaning: MP4 is a container that usually holds H.264 video and AAC sound. It plays on phones, computers, TVs and the web.
example: The video you send on a messaging app is an MP4.
vukem: The default export is an MP4 (H.264 and AAC), checked after it is made.

tip: Apple's QuickTime container, common in cameras and editing.
meaning: MOV is related to MP4 and is often used by iPhones and professional cameras and by editing programs on Mac.
example: A video recorded with an iPhone may be a .mov file.

tip: A flexible container that can hold many sound tracks and subtitles.
meaning: Matroska (MKV) is an open container with room for many audio tracks and subtitle tracks. Movie files often use it.
example: A movie file with three languages and four subtitle options.

tip: An open video format made for the web.
meaning: WebM is a container that holds VP9 or AV1 video and Opus or Vorbis sound. It can also keep see-through backgrounds.
example: A video with a transparent background to place on a web page.

tip: A short, silent, looping animation with few colours.
meaning: A GIF is a series of small pictures that loop. It has no sound and at most 256 colours, which is why it looks grainy, but it works everywhere.
example: A looping reaction image in a chat.
vukem: `--format gif` exports the composed frames, with no audio.

tip: The most used video codec in the world.
meaning: H.264 (also called AVC) gives small files with good quality and plays on practically every device. It is the safe choice.
example: Most videos you watch online are H.264.
vukem: The MP4 export uses an H.264 encoder.

tip: A newer codec that makes files about half as big as H.264, with more work.
meaning: H.265 (HEVC) saves more space, especially for 4K. It needs more computer power, and not every device or website plays it.
example: A 4K phone video saved in HEVC takes less space.

tip: A free codec made by Google, used by YouTube.
meaning: VP9 is an open codec with no fees. It saves space compared with H.264 and plays in browsers.
example: YouTube sends VP9 to browsers that can play it.

tip: A new free codec that makes small files with good quality.
meaning: AV1 is made by many big companies together. It is very efficient but slow to encode.
example: A streaming service sending AV1 saves internet data.

tip: A high-quality codec for editing, with big files.
meaning: ProRes keeps more detail and is easy for computers to edit, so professionals use it while working. The files are large.
example: A film crew edits in ProRes, then exports a small H.264 for the web.

tip: A codec made for editing, not for sending.
meaning: An intermediate codec is easy to cut and keeps quality through many steps. Files are large, so they are not for the web.
example: Converting phone videos to a smoother format before a big edit.

tip: The common audio codec of MP4 videos.
meaning: AAC squeezes sound into a small file and sounds good. Almost every device can play it.
example: The sound inside most phone videos.
vukem: MP4 exports have AAC sound. `--format aac` exports the sound only, as an `.m4a` file.

tip: The classic music file that made songs small enough to share.
meaning: MP3 is an older audio codec that squeezes music by dropping sounds that ears hardly hear.
example: A song from the early internet days.

tip: A modern, free audio codec for voice and music.
meaning: Opus works well for voice calls and for music, and is free to use. Browsers and many apps support it.
example: A voice call on the web.

tip: A file with sound that is not squeezed, so it keeps full quality.
meaning: WAV holds raw (PCM) sound. It sounds perfect but files are large. Editors use it to exchange sound.
example: A voice recording used as the master copy.
vukem: `--format wav` exports the audio mix as 16-bit PCM, 48 kHz, stereo.

tip: A way to squeeze sound without losing anything.
meaning: FLAC makes sound files smaller, and when you unpack them you get back every bit of the original.
example: A music collection kept at CD quality but using half the space.

tip: Lossy throws away details to be small; lossless keeps everything.
meaning: Lossy compression (like H.264 or MP3) removes things people hardly notice, and cannot be undone. Lossless (like FLAC or PNG) can be perfectly unpacked, but files are bigger.
example: Saving the same photo again and again as JPEG makes it worse each time.

tip: Making a file smaller by storing the same thing in fewer bits.
meaning: Compression finds repeated or unimportant parts and stores them more cleverly. In video, a still background is stored once, not 30 times a second.
example: A zip file is smaller than the folder inside it.

tip: How much data the video uses each second, like 8 Mbps.
meaning: A higher bitrate keeps more detail and makes a bigger file. A lower one makes a smaller file that may look blocky.
example: A video at 2 Mbps uses a quarter of the data of the same video at 8 Mbps.

tip: CBR uses the same data every second; VBR uses more when the picture is busy.
meaning: Constant bitrate (CBR) is steady and easy to stream. Variable bitrate (VBR) spends more on complicated moments and less on easy ones.
example: A calm interview needs fewer bits than an explosion.

tip: In compressed video, some frames are complete pictures and others only store changes.
meaning: An I-frame is a full picture. P and B frames store only what changed from other frames. That is how video gets small.
example: A talking head: only the lips and eyes change from frame to frame.

tip: A group of frames that begins with a complete picture.
meaning: A group of pictures (GOP) starts with an I-frame and has the following P and B frames. Seeking is quick when the groups are short.
example: A video that starts playing instantly when you drag the bar has short groups.

tip: How the colour of each pixel is stored, like yuv420p.
meaning: The pixel format says how many numbers describe each pixel and how they are arranged. Players need it to show the right colours.
example: yuv420p is the safest choice for videos that must play everywhere.
vukem: MP4 exports are verified, including the pixel format. See [Exporting](/docs/guide/exporting).

tip: Progressive shows whole pictures; interlaced shows two half-pictures of alternate lines.
meaning: Old TVs sent every other line (interlaced) to save data. Modern video is almost always progressive: a full picture each time.
example: Interlaced video can show combing lines on moving things on a modern screen.

tip: Common names for how many pixels a video has.
meaning: HD is 1280x720, Full HD is 1920x1080 and 4K (UHD) is 3840x2160. More pixels give more detail, and more data.
example: A 4K video has four times the pixels of a Full HD video.

tip: Putting the file's "table of contents" at the front, so playing can start before it is downloaded.
meaning: An MP4 needs a small header to start playing. If it is at the end, the player waits for the whole file. Fast start moves it to the beginning.
example: A video on a web page that starts at once instead of loading first.
vukem: The export checks that an MP4 has fast start.

tip: One kind of data inside a file, such as the video or one sound.
meaning: A file has several streams: a video stream, one or more audio streams, maybe a subtitle stream. Streaming also means sending video over the internet while it plays.
example: A movie with a video stream and two audio streams, English and Spanish.
vukem: An MP4 export is checked to have both streams and the right duration.

tip: Using the computer's special video chip to compress faster.
meaning: Graphics cards and phones have chips made to encode video quickly. They are faster than software, but sometimes slightly less efficient.
example: A phone exports a video in a few seconds using its chip.

tip: A free program that reads, converts and writes almost every video and sound format.
meaning: FFmpeg is the toolbox behind many video apps. It decodes and encodes formats and it can run from the command line.
example: A website that converts your video quickly is probably using FFmpeg.
vukem: Vukem Video uses an LGPL build of FFmpeg as a separate process. See [FFmpeg and licences](/docs/self-hosting/ffmpeg-and-licences).

tip: A video stored as many numbered pictures, one per frame.
meaning: Some programs save every frame as its own image file (frame0001.png, frame0002.png...). It keeps full quality and is used for animation and effects.
example: A 3D animation exported as 240 images for a 10-second clip at 24 fps.

tip: A file format to move an edit from one editing program to another.
meaning: OTIO describes the timeline (clips, tracks, times) without the media. Different programs can read it, so you can change tools.
example: Starting an edit in one program and finishing in another.

tip: A picture format that keeps full quality and can be see-through.
meaning: PNG compresses without losing anything and supports transparency. It is good for logos, screenshots and single frames.
example: A logo with a transparent background.
vukem: `--format png` exports one frame, chosen with `--at`.
